question: Potato cultivation is a key pillar of the economy of the Kato Nevrokopi basin and the main source of income for hundreds of family farms in the border area. The name ‘Kato Nevrokopi Potato’ is registered as a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI), recognising the special quality characteristics and the link of the product with its place of production.

However, according to complaints from producers and cooperatives, the availability of imported potatoes or those originating from other regions with unclear or misleading indications of origin makes it difficult to distinguish the authentic product, squeezes producer prices and undermines the added value of the PGI.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 strengthens the protection of geographical indications by providing for official controls and obliging the competent authorities to prevent and stop illegal or misleading uses of protected names. Accordingly: 1.

Does the Commission intend, in cooperation with the Greek authorities, to strengthen official controls on the marketing of fresh potatoes in order more effectively to prevent any abusive or misleading use of the name ‘Kato Nevrokopi Potato’?
Is the Commission considering measures to further strengthen the traceability of fresh agricultural products, so that the country and region of production can be directly verified?
Can digital traceability and PGI promotional activity be financed through the CAP or other EU programmes for the benefit of local producers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.11.2026) According to the legal framework1, it is for Member States to carry out controls on geographical indications (GIs) and it is required that Member States designate the competent authorities responsible for the verification of, and enforcement actions on, the use of GIs after the product designated by a GI has been placed on the market.

Enforcement actions concerning GIs may also be pursued by other authorities, such as customs and police, or directly by GI producer groups themselves. In addition, general labelling rules2 provide that food information must not mislead the consumer and not be ambiguous or confusing.

In line with the Commission’s Vision for Agriculture and Food3 commitment to reinforce country of origin labelling, the Commission proposal for the future Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) includes an amendment to the Common Market Organisation (CMO) Regulation4 that would allow such extension to new sectors.

The fresh fruit and vegetables sector (that does not include potatoes) is already subject to such an obligation of labelling of origin under marketing standards laid down according to Article 75 of the CMO Regulation.

The intervention ‘Quality Systems for Agricultural Products and Food4’5 under the Greek CAP Strategic Plan provides support for additional elements related to traceability included in specific quality schemes6. In all cases, however, the general traceability requirements for food safety purposes laid down in Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 (general Food Law Regulation)7 continue to apply.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1143 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 on geographical

indications for wine, spirit drinks and agricultural products, as well as traditional specialities guaranteed and optional quality terms for agricultural products, amending Regulations (EU) No 1308/2013, (EU) 2019/787 and (EU) 2019/1753 and repealing Regulation (EU) No 1151/2012 (OJ L, 2024/1143, 23.4.2024).

And Regulation (EU) 2017/625 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 15 March 2017 on official controls and other official activities performed to ensure the application of food and feed law, rules on animal health and welfare, plant health and plant protection products (Official Controls Regulation) (OJ L 95, 7.4.2017, p. 1).

2 Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, amending Regulations (EC) No 1924/2006 and (EC) No 1925/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council, and repealing Commission Directive 87/250/EEC, Council Directive 90/496/EEC, Commission Directive 1999/10/EC, Directive 2000/13/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council, Commission Directives 2002/67/EC and 2008/5/EC and Commission Regulation (EC) No 608/2004 (OJ L 304, 22.

11.2011, pp. 18–63). 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52025DC0075. 4 Regulation (EU) No 1308/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 December 2013 establishing a common organisation of the markets in agricultural products and repealing Council Regulations (EEC) No 922/72, (EEC) No 234/79, (EC) No 1037/2001 and (EC) No 1234/2007 (OJ L 347, 20.12.

7 Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 January 2002 laying down the general principles and requirements of food law, establishing the European Food Safety Authority and laying down procedures in matters of food safety (OJ L 31, 1.2.2002, pp.1-24).

The promotion of PGI quality schemes, including for the benefit of local producers, can be financed under Regulation (EU) No 1144/2014, namely through Work Programmes for promotion of agri-food products8.
